body: This is called the lipstick effect.
Some people call it lipstick syndrome.
The theory starts with a simple tradeoff.
In hard times, shoppers cut costly luxuries first.
But a small beauty treat may still feel affordable.
Lipstick became a symbol of that smaller indulgence.
After the 2001 downturn, Leonard Lauder noticed stronger lipstick sales.
He called it a lipstick index.
Researchers later tested the idea with mixed results.
Some found cosmetics spending rose for certain groups during recession.
Others found lipstick was not a reliable economic signal.
So the effect is better seen as consumer psychology than a forecast.

full_narration: While I count market money, economics explains why lipstick tempts us when budgets shrink. I reach for an economics guide, and the pattern opens. This is called the lipstick effect. Some people call it lipstick syndrome. The theory starts with a simple tradeoff. In hard times, shoppers cut costly luxuries first. A new car can wait. So can a big holiday. But a small beauty treat may still feel affordable. Lipstick became a symbol of that smaller indulgence. After the 2001 downturn, Leonard Lauder noticed stronger lipstick sales. He called it a lipstick index. Researchers later tested the idea with mixed results. Some found cosmetics spending rose for certain groups during recession. Others found lipstick was not a reliable economic signal. So the effect is better seen as consumer psychology than a forecast. When big luxuries vanish, small ones can feel more powerful.
